headline: Apple's macOS Tahoe code reveals new iPhones, AirPods, HomePod, and more
summary: References to iPhone 18 models, camera-equipped AirPods, and a Home Hub with a seven-inch display have been discovered within Apple's latest macOS release candidate.
details: Apple's macOS Tahoe 27.6 release candidate has inadvertently leaked details about numerous unannounced products. Codenames within the code suggest upcoming iPhone models, including the iPhone 18, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Ultra (reportedly a folding device), and a new iPhone Air 2.

The leak also points to new audio hardware, with references to camera-equipped AirPods, two new Beats headphone models, and AirPods Pro 4 earbuds. A codename N109 could indicate a second-generation Vision Pro headset, and ATVRemote1 may signal a new Apple TV remote and device.

Home accessories are also featured, with codenames J490 and B525 potentially referring to an upcoming Home Hub and HomePod Mini. The Home Hub is rumored to have a seven-inch display and a new homeOS, while the HomePod Mini is expected to support updated Siri features powered by Apple Intelligence.

Further details suggest an iPad Mini with an OLED display and A19 Pro chip, alongside multiple Mac updates including new MacBook Pro models (possibly with an M6 chip) and an iMac. These findings lend significant credibility to existing rumors and offer a clearer picture of Apple's upcoming product pipeline.

While Apple has not officially announced these products or their release dates, the presence of these references in a release candidate build strongly suggests their imminent arrival. Most of these devices are anticipated to be unveiled at Apple's traditional September iPhone event.

headline: AI-generated bills cause chaos in US Capitol, lawyers swamped with errors
summary: Congressional lawyers are reportedly spending more time fixing AI-generated legislative proposals than writing them from scratch due to errors and missed nuances.
details: US House lawyers are struggling with AI-generated bills that contain incorrect terms and citations, according to Politico. Offices are increasingly using tools like ChatGPT and Claude for drafting legislative proposals.

The House Office of Legislative Counsel (OLC) is reportedly spending more time reviewing and rewriting these AI-drafted bills than if they had started from scratch. AI tools often miss crucial nuances, leading to potential misinterpretations of laws.

Experts note that AI struggles with precise legal classifications, such as distinguishing between tax credits, deductions, or grants. It can also incorrectly define terms like 'state,' potentially excluding entities like DC or tribal nations from federal programs.
Beyond factual errors, AI-generated drafts may hinder staffers' understanding of the legislation. Relying on AI for drafting can mean not learning the issue as deeply as required.

To combat the increased workload, the OLC is exploring its own AI tools. A working group has developed 'Comparative Print Suite' to help visualize how proposals alter existing laws, with built-in error detection to prevent AI hallucinations.
